one_liner: Packed, immutable 2D R-tree and k-d tree crate (Rust port of flatbush/kdbush); builds about 2x faster than rstar bulk_load.
what_it_does: geo-index is a Rust crate (plus the geoindex-rs Python package) with a static 2D R-tree over axis-aligned boxes and a static 2D k-d tree over points. You size an RTreeBuilder with the item count, add() each box, then finish::<HilbertSort>() or finish::<STRSort>(); queries (search for box windows, neighbors for nearest items, intersection candidates against another tree) return u32 insertion indexes, not your objects. The whole tree lives in one Vec<u8> in the flatbush/kdbush byte layout, so it can be persisted, reopened zero-copy with RTreeRef::try_new, and shared with the JavaScript libraries or Python. It is not a drop-in for rstar: there is no insert or remove, no generic RTreeObject trait and no n-dimensional support.
how_it_is_fast: Construction is a bulk pack: item centers are mapped onto a 65,536 x 65,536 grid and sorted by Hilbert curve value (the threadlocalmutex bit-twiddling Hilbert function), or by sort-tile-recursive, and then parent boxes are computed bottom-up so every node is full except the last on each level. Sorting only has to order whole node-sized blocks (k_block_sort_by with select_nth_unstable_by), not the full array. Boxes and indices sit in flat contiguous arrays, so search is a breadth-first scan of 4-value box runs with no pointer chasing; the search loop skips bounds checks with get_unchecked, which a code comment credits with up to 30%. The optional rayon feature parallelizes the STR y-sort (STR construction 116.5 ms to 72.1 ms in the README).
when_to_use: Static 2D box or point sets (map features, tile footprints, GeoArrow geometries) built once and queried many times from Rust or Python
Bulk construction is on the critical path: the README run builds a Hilbert-packed tree in 80.9 ms vs 159.3 ms for rstar::RTree::bulk_load on the same boxes
You need to persist an index or pass it across an FFI/process boundary without serialization: the single-buffer flatbush layout reopens zero-copy and is readable by flatbush/kdbush in JS
Memory must be predictable: RTreeMetadata gives the exact byte size for a given item count and node size before you build
Nearest-neighbor ranking with your own metric (Manhattan, spherical with valid bounds) via neighbors_with_callbacks, without pulling in the geo crate
when_not_to_use: Data that changes after build: there is no insert or delete, so every update means a full rebuild; rstar supports dynamic updates
3D or higher-dimensional data: only two dimensions are indexed
Coordinates outside i8/u8/i16/u16/i32/u32/f32/f64 (no u64/i64), or data containing NaN, which the docs say may panic
You want the tree to hold and return your objects: queries return insertion indexes and you keep the collection yourself
You need k-nearest queries on the k-d tree: KDTree offers range and within (radius) only; kNN for the k-d tree is an open issue (#97)

integration.dependencies: bytemuck, float_next_after, geo-traits 0.3, num-traits, thiserror, tinyvec; optional rayon (parallel STR sort) and geo 0.31 (use-geo_0_31 feature for geometry distance APIs)
integration.platforms: any platform Rust targets; no SIMD or architecture-specific code seen. Python bindings published on PyPI as geoindex-rs
integration.thread_safety: not documented. The built RTree/KDTree is an immutable Vec<u8> plus metadata and queries take &self, so concurrent reads look safe, but the docs do not say so
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: replaces rstar::RTree::bulk_load plus envelope-intersection and nearest-neighbor queries for static 2D data, but with a different API (builder with a preset item count, index-returning queries) and no insert/remove or custom object types

gotchas: RTreeIndex::neighbors(x, y, max_results, max_distance) ranks by squared Euclidean distance and compares that against max_distance without squaring it (upstream flatbush squares maxDistance), so pass the squared radius there; neighbors_with_distance with EuclideanDistance takes a plain radius
RTreeBuilder::new takes the exact item count up front and finish() asserts that exactly that many boxes were added
The README calls it safe Rust, but the hot search loop uses unsafe get_unchecked, and RTreeRef::new_unchecked skips buffer validation; use try_new for untrusted buffers
Open issue #148: KDTree::within uses x^2 + y^2 <= r^2, which loses precision for extremely small coordinates and radii (e.g. 1e-308)
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over KDBush or RBush when you are in Rust or Python rather than JavaScript but still want the flatbush/kdbush buffer format, and it adds a box R-tree that KDBush lacks. Pick GeoToolbox KdBoxTree or ArborX instead for 3D+ data or C++ code, and tidwall/rtree.c or Boost R*-tree when the data must be updated in place.
verified_claims_summary: One first-party Criterion run (benches/rtree.rs) on a single bundled box dataset (benches/bounds.raw) shows Hilbert-packed construction at 80.9 ms vs 159.3 ms for rstar bulk_load (1.97x, derived from page data) and one fixed bounding-box query at 116.4 us vs 153.6 us (1.32x, derived from page data); CPU, rustc version and build profile are not stated. The rstar build closure also clones its input Vec inside the timed loop, and per GitHub's blame view the README timings date from a 2023 'Quick bench' commit, so they predate the v0.3.2 search optimization and do not name the rstar version used.
status_note: Active (v0.4.0 released 2026-09-09, last commit 2026-09-15, now under the georust org), dual MIT/Apache-2.0 licensed and published on crates.io and PyPI, with recent fixes for stack overflows, empty-tree panics and kNN distance bugs.
